Attacked on translation drift, which is where this track dies, and it held. I did not take the verifier's word for the scan: I downloaded the full text of the Clarendon Bailey myself (archive.org, onnatureofthings01lucruoft) and read the passage. The title page is 'LUCRETIUS ON THE NATURE OF THINGS, TRANSLATED BY CYRIL BAILEY, FELLOW OF BALLIOL COLLEGE, OXFORD AT THE CLARENDON PRESS'. Under the running head BOOK II the sentence comes back word for word: 'Thus the sum of things is ever being replenished, and mortals live one and all by give and take. Some races wax and others wane, and in a short space the tribes of living things are changed, and like runners hand on the torch of life.' The proposal takes the second sentence whole and changes nothing.

THE LOCATOR IS RIGHT, AND THE PRECEDING SENTENCE IS WHAT PROVES IT. The Latin at this point is 'sic rerum summa novatur semper, et inter se mortales mutua vivunt' (II.75 to 76), then 'augescunt aliae gentes, aliae minuuntur, inque brevi spatio mutantur saecla animantum et quasi cursores vitai lampada tradunt' (II.77 to 79). Bailey's 'Thus the sum of things is ever being replenished, and mortals live one and all by give and take' is 75 to 76 and the proposal correctly does not take it; what it takes begins at augescunt and ends at tradunt, which is 77 to 79 exactly. The famous torch is vitai lampada tradunt, the line Bailey renders 'hand on the torch of life', so the English and the Latin end at the same word.

WHAT I TRIED AND COULD NOT MAKE STICK. (1) Wrong Bailey. Bailey translated Lucretius twice, the 1910 Clarendon prose and the 1947 three-volume edition, and a proposal that quoted the later revision under the 1910 date would be a false citation. It does not: the wording I found is in the Clarendon prose volume the source names. (2) Verse run as prose. Rule 7 forbids running verse together as prose, and De Rerum Natura is hexameter, so this looked like the kill. It is not, because rule 7 binds the lineation of the edition named, and the edition named is a continuous prose translation with no lineation to keep. The house has already settled this case: month 03 ships 'Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 289 to 292 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914)', a verse work in a prose translation, quoted as prose, while month 02 ships Shantideva in a verse translation with slashes. The proposal is on the right side of that line. (3) The tag. I expected to break it here, since the house tags verse works Poetry (Hesiod, Horace, Dante, Virgil). But month 02 ships 'Shantideva, The Way of the Bodhisattva, chapter 8, verse 129' as Philosophy, so a philosophical poem tagged Philosophy is house practice, and De Rerum Natura is the didactic poem of Epicurean philosophy. Philosophy stands. It is the editor's call if the month's tag balance wants it moved, not a defect in the citation. (4) Misattribution. Lucretius is on no trap list and the torch is his, not a proverb; the English tag 'hand on the torch' descends from this very line. (5) Publishability. The context is generations replacing one another, not dying bodies; nothing in the sentence needs a warning, and at six in the morning the runners handing on the torch is the consoling half of impermanence, which is what the August blurb asks for.

EVERY OTHER GATE. shipped.js on the exact line: shipped [], near [], lucretius at 0 of 3 for the year, cap 3, not banned, and he is on neither personsAtCap nor personsUsed, so he costs the month nothing and adds a Roman first century BC voice. Source line 'Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book II, lines 77 to 79 (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1910)' is 78 characters, leads with the author's name, gives work then book and lines then translator and year, no dash, no straight quote. The quotation ends in a full stop and contains no quote marks. Scope is clear on every head, and a translation of 1910 is long before the 1999 line.

ONE HONEST FOOTNOTE, NOT A REFUTATION. The scan I read is a later Clarendon impression, not the 1910 sheets: its imprint page carries Humphrey Milford and Amen House, E.C.4, which dates the printing to the middle 1920s at the earliest. Bailey's translation is the same translation, first published 1910, and rule 4 asks for the year of the published translation whose wording is used, so 1910 is the right year to print. I record it only so that nobody later mistakes the scan for the first impression. The verifier's claim to have read 'the scanned text of Bailey's translation, Oxford at the Clarendon Press, 1910' is true of the translation and loose about the impression.
